newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe court orders frequencies for mobile phones.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe court orders frequencies for mobile phones.

text.p: Zimbabwe's supreme court ordered the government of President Robert Mugabe on Wednesday to outline within the next three weeks frequencies in which private mobile cellular telephone services can be operated.
Chief Justice Anthony Gubbay said the government's year-long delay seemed vindictive and aimed at ensuring the state Posts and Telecommunications (PTC) enjoyed a monopoly in this sector.

In agreement with four other high court judges, he was passing judgment on an appeal by a Zimbabwean firm, T.S. Masiyiwa Holdings, which said the state's conduct and presidential rules barring operators without state specified frequencies had prejudiced its plans to establish a cellular phone service.

The government announced the new rules in February, a month after T.S. Masiyiwa had won a historic court challenge to have the state monopoly on the provision of cellular telephones declared unconstitutional after it was denied a licence to operate such a service.
The company had already set up its system and was ready to provide a service to some 5,000 customers.

The PTC launched its own cellular telephone service in October which it said would initially cover the southern African country's major cities of Harare, Bulawayo, Mutare and Kwekwe -- the areas T.S Masiyiwa Holdings' subsidiary Econet had targeted.
Ordering the Minister of Information, Posts and Telecommunications, Joyce Mujuru, to prepare frequency specifications by no later than January 14, 1997, Chief Justice Gubbay said:
"Section 24 (4) (of the Constitution) allows the Supreme Court a wide and unfettered discretion for the purpose of enforcing fundamental human rights and freedoms of the individual".
"Failure to comply with the time limits would deem the applicant (T.S. Masiyiwa's Econet) immediately licensed for a period of three years.

"There is a distinct element of unfairness in the delay. It is sympotomatic of an absence of respect for the right of others to establish a mobile cellular service in Zimbabwe and of the corresponding right of the public to enjoy that facility other than through the Corporation (PTC)," he added.
